title: Single-Cycle Datapath
summary: Building a complete datapath where every instruction fully completes in one clock cycle, and why that's simpler but wasteful.

slides.markdown:
A **single-cycle datapath** completes an entire instruction — fetch, decode, execute, memory access, write-back — within **one clock cycle**, no matter what kind of instruction it is. There's no partial state carried between cycles for one instruction; each cycle starts and finishes a whole instruction.

This makes the design conceptually simple: you can point at the hardware and say "here is fetch, here is decode, here is execute," all wired together and active simultaneously for whatever instruction is currently running. The simplicity comes at a real cost, covered ahead.

All the major components connect in one wired path that a single instruction flows through completely:

![The full single-cycle datapath: PC, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory, and muxes](assets/single-cycle-datapath.svg)

Every component is present for every instruction, even ones that don't need it — a register-register `add` still has wires running through the data memory block, they're just unused that cycle. That's the source of the design's inefficiency, made concrete.

assets.alt: The full single-cycle datapath: PC, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory, and muxes

slides.markdown:
The datapath has one fixed wiring, but different instructions need different data flowing through it — an `add` needs a register operand for the ALU's second input, while `addi` needs an immediate instead. **Multiplexers (muxes)** are how the same wires serve both.

Each mux picks between two or more inputs based on a **control signal** derived from the opcode: "ALU second operand — register or immediate?", "write-back value — ALU result or memory data?" Muxes are the datapath's decision points; the control unit ([control-unit-design](control-unit-design)) is what sets their selector bits.

Because every instruction must finish in one clock cycle, the cycle length must be **long enough for the slowest instruction** to complete — typically a `load`, which chains fetch → decode → address computation → memory access → write-back, the longest path through the hardware.

A simple register-register `add` finishes its actual work far faster, but it still gets the *same* long cycle as the load — the clock can't run faster for some instructions and slower for others. Every simple instruction wastes time waiting out a cycle sized for the worst case.

Tracing `add $t2, $t0, $t1` through the datapath in one cycle:

```
1. Fetch:   PC reads instruction word from instruction memory
2. Decode:  opcode -> ALU op = ADD
            register file reads $t0 and $t1
3. Execute: ALU computes $t0 + $t1
4. Memory:  unused for this instruction (no load/store)
5. Write-back: ALU result written into $t2
```

All five steps happen within the same clock cycle, in this order, purely by wiring — there's no "waiting" between steps; signals simply propagate through combinational logic until they settle.

The trade this design makes:

| | Single-cycle | Multi-cycle |
|---|---|---|
| Design complexity | Simple — one path, one cycle | More complex — needs internal state/FSM |
| Clock period | Fixed at the slowest instruction's time | Can vary — shorter, per-step cycles |
| Hardware reuse | None — separate resources per stage | Shares one ALU/memory across steps |
| Efficiency | Wastes time on simple instructions | Better matches time to actual work |

Single-cycle is the natural first design to learn, but essentially no real CPU ships this way — it's a stepping stone to [multi-cycle-datapath](multi-cycle-datapath) and eventually pipelining.

slides.subTitle: Assuming equal instruction time
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Since the clock is fixed, every instruction in a single-cycle datapath naturally takes about the same real time."

**Why it's wrong:** the clock period is fixed, but it's set by the **slowest** instruction's critical path (typically loads). A fast instruction like a register-register `add` finishes its actual logic well before the cycle ends and simply sits idle for the remainder.

**Correct model:** the slowest instruction sets the clock for everyone — "equal time per cycle" doesn't mean "equal useful work per cycle." This wasted time is exactly what motivates multi-cycle and pipelined designs.

slides.subTitle: A worked example
slides.markdown:
```text
Component delays (illustrative): instruction memory=200ps, register read=100ps,
ALU=150ps, data memory=250ps, register write=50ps

add's critical path:  200 (fetch) + 100 (reg read) + 150 (ALU) + 50 (reg write)
                     = 500ps

lw's critical path:   200 (fetch) + 100 (reg read) + 150 (ALU, addr calc)
                       + 250 (data memory) + 50 (reg write)
                     = 750ps

Clock period = max(500, 750, ...all instruction types...) = 750ps
```

`add` could in principle run at 500ps, but the single shared clock must accommodate `lw`'s longer path, so every instruction — including `add` — pays the full 750ps every cycle. This is the exact number multi-cycle and pipelined designs are built to stop wasting.

slides.subTitle: One memory can't serve two masters in the same cycle
slides.markdown:
A `load` instruction, in a single cycle, must both **fetch its own instruction word** and **read its data operand from memory** — two separate memory accesses in the same clock cycle. A single, unified memory with one port physically cannot service both requests simultaneously.

This is why single-cycle (and most simple textbook) datapaths use **separate instruction and data memories** (a Harvard-style split, at least at the L1 level) rather than one unified memory — it's not a stylistic choice, it's forced by the constraint that instruction fetch and a load/store's data access must both complete within one shared cycle. Multi-cycle designs, by contrast, can get away with a single memory port precisely because fetch and data access happen in different cycles and never need it at the same time.
